papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc. web lesson that explains the P and NP classes, NP-completeness, NP-hardness, their caveats for real optimization work, and the expert view on quantum algorithms and NP-hard optimization.

assertions.value: The authors state that, informally, the conjecture that P does not equal NP says that optimization problems exist that cannot be solved to optimality quickly, no matter how clever an algorithm is.
quotes: there are optimization problems in existence that cannot be solved (to optimality) quickly, no matter how clever an algorithm is.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states its own informal definition of the conjecture in the first section.

assertions.value: The authors state that the informal statement of the conjecture is not mathematically rigorous, and that complexity theory must be explained in detail to show what it does and does not tell us.
quotes: While this statement may be intuitively clear, it is not mathematically rigorous.
It is as important to understand what complexity theory tells us, but it is also very important to understand what it doesn't tell us.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states the scope of its own informal statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that the claim that hard optimization problems exist is a conjecture rather than a proven statement, because a proof would have to consider every possible method to solve them.
quotes: it is easy to see why this is a conjecture rather than a proven statement
would have to consider every possible method to solve them
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal argument by the authors, without a proof in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that hard problems in NP can be mapped into each other, so an efficient algorithm for one problem in the hardest class would show that none of them are hard in a particular formal sense.
quotes: can be mapped into each other, a demonstration that an efficient algorithm exists for one problem in the hardest class of problems is also a demonstration that none of them are hard
assertions.certainty_reason: A textbook result stated informally without proof in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that the enormous amount of work on optimization algorithms, together with the easier route to a proof of equality than of inequality, has led to an informal consensus among experts that P does not equal NP.
quotes: the enormous amount of work that has gone into the study of optimization algorithms has led to an informal consensus among experts that
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of expert opinion with no survey or citation in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that NP stands for non-deterministic polynomial time, and that a frequent error is to state that NP stands for non-polynomial.
assertions.anchor: What the letters P and NP mean, web lesson
quotes: non-deterministic polynomial time
Note that a frequent error is to state that N P NP NP stands for
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines the class names in its own words.

assertions.value: The authors define a problem as in P when the time to solve it, using an algorithm that can run on a classical non-quantum computer, grows only polynomially with the number of variables.
quotes: means that the time to solve a problem (using some algorithm which can be run on a classical i.e. non-quantum computer)
only grows polynomially with
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines the class P in its own words.

assertions.value: The authors state that growth can be slower than exponential but faster than polynomial, and that an algorithm with such growth cannot solve a problem in polynomial time.
quotes: Growth can be slower than exponential but faster than polynomial
Such an algorithm therefore cannot solve a problem in polynomial time
assertions.certainty_reason: A textbook statement given without a proof in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors define a problem as in NP when it can be solved in polynomial time if one gets maximally lucky guessing solutions, with the added requirement that the quality of an answer can be verified efficiently.
quotes: if it can be solved in polynomial time if you get maximally lucky guessing solutions
we have to be able to efficiently (polynomially increasing time with the problem size) verify the quality of our answer from guessing
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines the class NP in its own words.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson describes NP through lucky guessing and verification, which is an informal form of the standard definition.

assertions.value: The authors state that if P equals NP then any optimization problem that could be solved quickly by getting maximally lucky could also be solved quickly without that benefit, while the suspected case of inequality means at least some optimization problems will not be fast to solve by any method.
quotes: any optimization problem that could be solved "quickly" by getting maximally lucky could also be solved quickly without this benefit
at least some optimization problems will not be fast to solve by any method
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal restatement of the conjecture, not a proof.

assertions.value: The authors give the traveling salesperson problem as an example of a problem solvable in polynomial time by maximally lucky guessing: one guesses the order of the cities, and the length of the route can be verified quickly with a simple calculation.
quotes: you just guess the order of the cities
The length of this route could also be quickly verified, with a simple and fast calculation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An illustrative example in a tutorial, not a derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that all optimization problems with efficiently calculable objective functions are verifiable, but other kinds of problems, such as counting problems, are not.
quotes: All optimization problems with efficiently calculable objective functions are verifiable, but other kinds of problems aren't.
Some examples here are counting problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement given without proof in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that the #SAT counting problem is not in NP, because even with maximally lucky guesses the satisfying strings must be counted one by one, and an efficient verification of a decision version would not be possible.
assertions.anchor: NP and Optimization versus decision problems, web lesson
quotes: Getting maximally lucky means you can find a new string satisfying the conditions very quickly, but they still need to be counted one by one.
no such efficient verification would be possible, #SAT problems are therefore said to not be
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal argument in a tutorial, not a proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that the problems complexity theory usually deals with are decision problems with yes or no answers, and that optimization problems can be translated into decision problems.
assertions.anchor: Optimization versus decision problems, web lesson
quotes: The problems that complexity theory usually deals with are decision problems, with yes or no answers.
Optimization problems can be translated into decision problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states the scope of the problems that the theory treats.

assertions.value: The authors describe NP-complete problems as decision problems that can be efficiently solved by maximally lucky guessing and efficiently verified, and into which any other such problem can be mapped by a reduction whose time grows only polynomially with the problem size.
assertions.anchor: Optimization versus decision problems, web lesson
quotes: can be mapped into them in a time that scales only polynomially with the size of the problem
These mappings are known as reductions
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines NP-complete problems and reductions in its own words.

assertions.value: The authors state that the polynomial factors coming from reductions could be very detrimental to the performance of an algorithm in practice, and that this is a general weakness of complexity theory, which describes efficiency only in a very abstract sense.
assertions.anchor: Optimization versus decision problems, web lesson
quotes: In practice, the polynomial factors coming from these mappings could be very detrimental to the performance of an algorithm.
it tells us about efficiency only in a very abstract sense
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states a limit of the theory it describes.

assertions.value: The authors state that some problems appear to be hard but are not NP-complete, and that hardness, even for all algorithms, does not imply NP-completeness.
assertions.anchor: Optimization versus decision problems, web lesson
quotes: It is worth emphasizing that there are problems that appear to be hard but are not N P NP NP -complete.
does not imply N P NP NP -completeness
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement given without proof in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that programs on a universal computer can be reduced to a certain class of satisfiability problems, which are now known to be NP-complete, and that this is used to show all NP problems reduce to NP-complete problems.
assertions.anchor: Optimization versus decision problems, web lesson
quotes: This fact can be proven by showing that programs on a universal computer can be reduced to a certain class of satisfiability problems
assertions.certainty_reason: A known result that the lesson reports without a proof or a citation.

assertions.value: The authors define NP-hard problems as problems at least as hard as NP-complete problems, in the sense that NP-complete problems can be efficiently reduced to them, without the restriction of being decision problems and without a requirement that solutions be verifiable.
quotes: problems that are at least as hard as N P NP NP -complete problems (in the sense that N P NP NP -complete problems can be efficiently reduced to them)
There is also no requirement for N P NP NP -hard solutions to be verifiable in any way.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines NP-hard in its own words.

assertions.value: The authors state that NP-hard problems formally include some problems that are proven to be undecidable, such as the halting problem, and that such problems are excluded from the hard optimization problems of interest because they are not optimization problems.
quotes: they formally include some problems which are proven to be undecidable
Problems like the halting problem are excluded from this distinction by not being optimization problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A textbook statement given without proof in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hard optimization problems they are interested in are formally NP-hard optimization problems, meaning optimization problems at least as hard to solve as NP-complete decision problems.
quotes: optimization problems which are at least as hard to solve as N P NP NP -complete decision problems
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states the scope of the problems it treats.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in practice, technically incorrect shorthand terms are often used for hard optimization problems, and that the set of problems that are interesting in practice is cumbersome to define in a rigorous theoretical framework.
quotes: shorthand terms that are technically incorrect but generally clear from context are often used when discussing hard optimization problems
the set of problems that are interesting in practice are cumbersome to define within a rigorous theoretical framework
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states a limit on the precision of its own terminology.

assertions.value: The authors state that NP-hardness and NP-completeness are worst-case statements, so not all instances of an NP-hard or NP-complete problem will actually be hard, and for some problems typical cases are not hard.
quotes: so not all instances of an N P NP NP -hard or complete problem will actually be hard
In fact, for some problems, typical cases are not hard.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states a limit of what NP-hardness implies.

assertions.value: The authors state that video games such as Super Mario are formally NP-hard but typical gameplay does not require advanced optimization algorithms, because a level that is fun to play looks very different from one that maps a hard problem.
quotes: typical gameplay does not require advanced optimization algorithms
building a level that is fun to play looks very different from one that maps a hard problem
assertions.certainty_reason: An illustrative claim in a tutorial without evidence in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors report that early attempts to benchmark D-Wave quantum annealers used randomly assigned couplings within the restricted hardware graph, and that work in the spin glass community showed such problems were relatively easy for the Monte Carlo family of algorithms.
quotes: Early attempts to benchmark D-Wave quantum annealers were based on randomly assigned couplings within the restricted hardware graph
work done within the spin glass community showed that such problems were relatively easy for the Monte Carlo family of algorithms
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the lesson attributes to other work, with the citation lost in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson names no source in the text layer; the links were lost.

assertions.value: The authors state that algorithms that scale polynomially can become infeasible at certain sizes, and that a high-order polynomial such as n to the power 50 may as well be exponential for large n.
quotes: In practice, even algorithms that scale polynomially can become infeasible to use at certain sizes
a high-order polynomial like n 50 n^{50} n 50 may as well be exponential for large n n n
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states a limit of what polynomial scaling implies.

assertions.value: The authors state that reducing a runtime that is still super-polynomial can make a huge difference in practice, and that this is all any commercial optimization solver is able to do on hard instances of NP-hard optimization.
quotes: Reducing the runtime of a problem in a way where the runtime is still super-polynomial.
can actually make a huge difference in practice
This is all any commercial optimization solver is able to do on (hard instances of) N P NP NP -hard optimization
assertions.certainty_reason: An unreferenced statement about commercial solvers in a vendor tutorial.

assertions.value: The authors state that the theory tells us nothing about the prefactors on the scaling terms or about the size at which the scaling approximation becomes valid, and that scaling can be observed empirically but there is no guaranteed way to tell whether one is in the large-size limit.
quotes: the theory tells us nothing about the prefactors on the scaling terms or at what size the scaling approximation becomes valid
Scaling can be empirically observed, but there is no guaranteed way to tell if one is in the large-size limit.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states a limit of asymptotic scaling analysis.

assertions.value: The authors state that scaling only tells how an algorithm performs on very large problems, and that it is sometimes better in practice to use an algorithm that does not have the optimal scaling, or whose scaling is unknown.
quotes: Scaling only tells us how an algorithm performs on very large problems
it is sometimes better in practice to use an algorithm that is not the one with the optimal scaling, or even where the scaling is unknown
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states a limit of scaling analysis.

assertions.value: The authors state that nothing in the theory says that all hard optimization problems must be NP-hard, and that, assuming P does not equal NP, showing a problem is not NP-hard does not imply an algorithm with polynomial scaling.
quotes: nothing in the theory says that all hard optimization problems must be N P NP NP -hard
showing that a problem is not N P NP NP -hard does not imply an algorithm with polynomial scaling
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement given without proof in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that the reduction techniques used in computer science proofs tend to be designed to be general rather than efficient and are often not very useful in practice.
quotes: The reduction techniques used in computer science proofs tend to be designed to be general rather than efficient and are often not very useful in practice.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement without evidence in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that solving in the context of NP-hardness implies finding the single most optimal solution, that complexity theory for approximate solutions is not discussed in the lesson, and that in practice a good-quality approximate solution is often the goal.
quotes: implies finding the single most optimal solution
There is complexity theory relating to approximate solutions but we do not discuss it here.
In practice, finding a good-quality approximate solution is often the goal.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states the scope of its own treatment.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is widely believed among experts, though not formally proven, that P does not equal NP, that this belief rests on decades of research not finding an efficient algorithm for any of these problems, and that a single efficient algorithm for any NP-hard problem would show P equals NP.
quotes: Although not formally proven, it is widely believed among experts that
This belief is based on decades of research not finding an efficient algorithm for any of these problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of expert opinion with no survey or citation in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that an unclaimed one million dollar prize exists for a solution to the question of whether P equals NP.
quotes: There is an unclaimed one-million-dollar prize for a solution to this question
assertions.certainty_reason: An unreferenced statement in a vendor tutorial.

assertions.value: The authors state that experts widely agree that quantum algorithms will probably not be able to solve NP-hard optimization in polynomial time, and that this is a question about the relation between NP and BQP rather than about P versus NP, because the definition of P does not include quantum resources.
quotes: Experts widely agree that quantum algorithms will probably not be able to solve N P NP NP -hard optimization in polynomial time.
Formally the definition of P P P does not include quantum resources
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of expert opinion with no survey or citation in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors describe BQP as the class of problems efficiently solvable by quantum computers, and state that the belief rests on the advantage seen in simplified database search problems, which suggest but do not formally prove that a quantum algorithm can solve an optimization problem in the square root of the classical runtime but not exponentially faster.
quotes: the class of problems efficiently solvable by quantum computers
making an algorithm quantum can make an optimization problem solvable in the square root of the runtime of the classical equivalent
but not exponentially faster
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about a known quantum search speedup without a derivation or citation in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson refers to the Grover style square root speedup but does not name it.

assertions.value: The authors, a quantum computing company, state that the P versus NP problem is one of the main drivers of quantum computing and that understanding it explains why many unconventional computing approaches are valuable.
quotes: is one of the main drivers of quantum computing
why many unconventional computing approaches are so valuable in today's world
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing the motivation for its own field of products.
